title: Removing a foreign object (splinter, fishhook)
what: The doctor removes something stuck in your skin: a splinter, a piece of glass, or a fishhook. The area is numbed if needed.
why: When the object is deep, cannot be removed at home, is near the eye or on the face, or the area is getting inflamed.
tell_doctor: What exactly got into the skin and when
When you last had a tetanus shot
Allergy to numbing medicines or antiseptics

prepare.title: Do not pull it out yourself
prepare.text: A barbed hook or a deep shard is better not removed at home. You can make the wound bigger.

prepare.title: Before the visit
prepare.text: Do not touch the area. You can cover it with a clean bandage. Hold a large object in place so it does not move.

prepare.title: Eye
prepare.text: If something got into your eye, do not rub it. See a doctor right away.

bring: Your tetanus shot record, if you have it
steps: The doctor examines the area and decides how to remove the object
Sometimes an X-ray or ultrasound is done to find a shard
The skin is cleaned with antiseptic
If needed, a numbing injection is given
The object is carefully removed with an instrument
The wound is rinsed and covered with a bandage
feel: Then you feel pressure, but no pain
After the procedure, the spot may ache a little
after: Keep the wound clean and dry for the first 24 hours
Change the bandage as your doctor said
Sometimes the doctor gives a tetanus shot
red_flags: Redness is spreading, or the area is hot and more and more painful
Pus comes from the wound, or you get a fever
A finger or hand goes numb or does not move well

faq.q: Can I remove a fishhook myself?
faq.a: A small splinter near the surface, yes. A barbed hook is better left to a doctor, so the tissue is not torn.

faq.q: Do I need a tetanus shot?
faq.a: It depends on when you last had one. Your doctor will ask and decide.

reminders.text: Your visit is soon. Do not try to remove the object yourself, and keep the area clean.
